what_taken: Sydney, 2016 census, garden logbooks 2015-17: 13 gardens yielded 5.94 kg and 8515 kJ per m2 a year (p. 5). Verges, vacant land and 25% of yards would supply 15.0% of food energy for the 2.67 million people in the modelled blocks (71.1% of the 10 urban SA4s); 24.4% at 50% and 33.8% at 75% of yards (Table 4, p. 8). Labour limits every scenario (p. 9).

flags: A section 12 (forced local self-sufficiency: gardens, fruit and vegetables) and DISCUSSION_MEASURES D9 (gardens): if Sydney urban agriculture is cited, the 15% is food energy for the 2.67 million residents of the modelled blocks, not all of Greater Sydney (4.9 million, p. 5), and labour exceeds the population in every amateur scenario (p. 9); the authors rule out the 75% scenario and possibly the 50% (p. 10).
notes: File confirmed: Mcdougall, Rader, Kristiansen, Land Use Policy 94 (2020) 104554, doi:10.1016/j.landusepol.2020.104554 (p. 1). Method: yield, labour and inputs logged by 13 volunteer gardeners; available yard, verge and miscellaneous land measured on 0.3 m aerial imagery for 20 SA1 blocks chosen by stratified random sampling; linear models on population density and household income extrapolate to 6032 blocks (pp. 5, 8). Roofs excluded; 28% of land assumed contaminated, needing raised beds (p. 7). The title's 15% equals the 25% yard scenario; the 'or its entire vegetable supply' phrase rests on 15.8% of kJ equalling 107.5% of recommended vegetable intake (p. 8). Table 2 (pp. 3 to 4) is a review of 15 city studies, 1% to 30% of calories. Replaces 'title only'.

Method: Google Earth Engine; NDVI on Landsat 2009-11; building area regressed on Landscan population; vacant land from 15.4% US average reduced by density (high) or 1% (low); crop mix weighted by a 0-3 suitability rank on each country's FAO 2010 crop list; livestock excluded (pp. 42 to 45). No Australian figure in the text. McDougall 2020 (L183, p. 4) reports this paper as 1.5-2.8% of total global crop production (98 or 178 Mt over 6433 Mt).

what_taken: Global, 1996-2005 monthly climate, year-2000 cropland, 130 crops: 15% of cropland (0.14 billion ha) is rain-fed with renewable water to spare; irrigating it sustainably would feed 620 million more people, and up to 25% and 840 million with 50% deficit irrigation (p. 3; 620-840 million, 6-8% more calories, p. 7). Sustainable irrigation use is at most 810 against 1083 km3 a year consumed (p. 5).

notes: File confirmed: Rosa, Chiarelli, Rulli, Dell'Angelo, D'Odorico, Sci. Adv. 6 (2020) eaaz6031, 29 April 2020 (p. 1). Method: monthly agro-hydrological model at 5 arc min; crop water requirement from a daily soil water balance; renewable blue water from Composite Runoff V1.0 less environmental flows (Variable Monthly Flow method); added calories at attainable yields (Mueller et al.) with yields falling linearly under deficit irrigation (pp. 7 to 8). Exclusions stated: economic viability, nutrient limits, water quality and year-to-year variation in water availability (p. 8). Australia appears once: the Murray-Darling Basin is among irrigated regions facing blue water scarcity for several months (p. 3); high-income and arid regions hold little economically water scarce land (p. 4). Consistent with A section 11 (irrigation adds 0 to 2%) and DISCUSSION_MEASURES D6; changes neither.

what_taken: Review of 44 publications, 1980-2015, final energy, packaging and retail excluded, UK focus (p. 271). The food sector uses about 200 EJ a year globally, 45% in processing and distribution (p. 270). UK food processing used 117 PJ in 2017 (p. 270), 58% gas, 34% electricity (p. 276). Over 98% of UK food moves by road (p. 275). Instant coffee 50.2, crisps 17.3, milk powder 16.2 MJ/kg (p. 277).

flags: A section 7 and section 8 (liquid fuel settings), DISCUSSION_MEASURES D7 (farm diesel) and B section 8 (fossil energy): the paper covers manufacturing and distribution energy in the UK and globally; it gives no farm or on-farm fuel figure, no liquid fuel quantity per tonne-km in the main text (transport intensities are in Appendix I, not on file) and no Australian figure, so it supports a statement about post-farm energy, not the model's fuel settings.
notes: File confirmed: Ladha-Sabur, Bakalis, Fryer, Lopez-Quiroga, Trends in Food Science and Technology 86 (2019) 270-280, doi:10.1016/j.tifs.2019.02.034 (p. 270). Method: literature survey (ScienceDirect, Knovel), specific energy consumption in MJ per kg of product, grouped by period (before 2000, 2000-04, 2005-15), averages only where more than two values; data accuracy not reported in the sources (pp. 271 to 272, 276). what_taken: Maximum covariance analysis of 1980-2010 crop statistics (subnational for eight countries, Australian wheat from ABS; FAO elsewhere) against sea surface temperature: ENSO, IOD, tropical Atlantic and NAO explain 18, 7 and 6% of globally aggregated maize, soybean and wheat production variance, and 23, 15 and 17% of local variance (Global analysis). ENSO and IOD together explain 30 to 41% of wheat variability in Australia and East Africa (Regional analyses).

notes: File confirmed from the PubMed Central rendering: Anderson, Seager, Baethgen, Cane, You, 'Synchronous crop failures and climate-forced production variability', Sci. Adv. 5(7) eaaw1976, 2019, doi:10.1126/sciadv.aaw1976. The rendering has no page numbers, so sections are cited; its header fields 'fpage 458, lpage 469' and 'pub-date 72019' are rendering artefacts (458-469 are the pages of the paper's reference 1), and its abstract is the one-line teaser only. Method: yields detrended with a Gaussian filter (about a 9-year mean), production anomalies by harvested area, MCA by mode and season, ENSO removed before the regional modes (Materials and Methods). Only ENSO forces globally synchronous failures; wheat and soybean anomalies largely offset at global scale. Per-region Australian values are in Fig. 3, not in the text.
